subject: Feedback on speeding up slow, hierarchical model of test kinetics

messages.author: 4d17bc398c8d91b8
messages.subject: Feedback on speeding up slow, hierarchical model of test kinetics
parts:
Hi all,

I’m trying to figure out ways of making my (relatively complex but not obscenely so) model run better, and would greatly appreciate any help in that regard! I’m running Stan 2.4.0 via Rstan, using R 3.1.1 on OSX10.9.4, on a Macbook Pro 2ghz/16b RAM. 

 The (hierarchical) model has 1700 parameters in total  and 500 observations . It  is currently taking approximately 8hours per chain (run in parallel, so 8hrs total) for 5k iterations, but with runs varying in time from 4-8hours per chain. At that point, some parameters have ”converged”, with Rhat of  around 1, but _lp has an Rhat of 1.4, and 100/1700 parameters have Rhats of 2-4.
The model fit to the data is also kinda rubbish, but I suspect that’s down to some sillyness of my own with regards to the choice of priors. 

I tried looking at get_sampler_params: one of four chains seems to converge to a region with a small number of leapfrogs after ~3000 iterations (2^3 tree depth, 3-5 jumps); the other three are stuck around 2000. 

I’ve attached my model code. This is an attempt to replicate a model published in Stats in Medicine in 2009 (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sim.3592/abstract ) - I'm using their data, but only a third of the observations, to speed things up. Their model was implemented in WinBugs, and apparently ran relatively quickly.
  
Briefly, it's modelling three IG levels per patient, each patient being measured several times. The development of IG levels over time is described by a four-parameter function, with parameters X.star,S,a,D. This function is continuous, but have different behaviour if t<D or t>D, and so I'm using an if... else clause - I suspect this is a problem, but don't know how to go about it .

Again, any feedback would be much appreciated!

Best,
Gustaf

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feedback on speeding up slow, hierarchical model of test kinetics
parts:
Hi, Gustaf.  This is an unusual model in that you have a parameter with a prior scaled to 0.0001.  This might make sense in your example but in general we recommend scaling things so that parameters are of order of magnitude 1.  Regarding the discontinuity: it might be a good idea to try a fully continuous model and see how it goes.  Then if it goes fast, you’ll know that the problem is the discontinuity and you can think of ways of speeding things up (for example, making the model itself a bit more continuous, which, following the principle of the Folk Theorem, might even make it a better model) and if the continuous model is slow then you can continue to strip down the model until it runs fast, so you can figure out where the problem is.

Also you could try carefully choosing starting points.  This can make a difference, especially if some chains are going really slow.

Andrew

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Feedback on speeding up slow, hierarchical model of test kinetics
parts:
You want to use quad_form_diag instead of the diag_matrix construction.
It should be much more efficient. But the big speedup would be in
going to a cholesky factor parameterization rather than a covariance
matrix one.

Is that cauchy(0,0.0001) really meant to be the other way around and
be very diffuse? Stan uses scale parameters (1/precision^2) for distributions,
not precisions.

You could probably scrunch all those theta2IgLogmu priors into
a single vectorized call, with

to_vector(theta2IgLogmu[i]) ~ cauchy(0, 0.1);

Also, our multi_normal is now vectorized and generalized from column
vectors to also work on row vectors. So you shouldn't need the to_vector
on these:

for(i in 1:I){
...
for(n in 1:N){
to_vector(row(theta1IgLogmu[n],i))~multi_normal(to_vector(row(theta2IgLogmu,i)),igCov[i]);
}
}

To start, row(x,i) is longhand for x[i]. And you don't need the to_vector any more,
so this is all just:

for(i in 1:I){
...
for(n in 1:N){
theta1IgLogmu[n,i] ~ multi_normal(theta2IgLogmu[i] ,igCov[i]);
}
}


But what you really want to do for speed is transpose theta1IgLogmu by defining
theta1IgLogmu_t such that you can write the above as:

for(i in 1:I){
...
theta1IgLogmu_t[i] ~ multi_normal(theta2IgLogmu[i] ,igCov[i]);
}

You have to declare thetaIgLogMu_t as

vector[K] thetaIgLogMu_t[I,N];

and then use it so that

theta1IgLogmu_t[i,n,k] = theta1IgLogmu[n,i,k]

and so that theta1IgLogmu_t[i] is an array of vectors, which is what
you need in the argument position to vectorize.

There's a chapter in the manual explaining efficiency issues of
arrays vs. vectors/matrices.

Any of the variables in transformed parameters you don't want to
save can be declared as locals in the model block (or in the transformed
parameters block if you need them later in the transformed param block
but not in the model).

You might also find it helpful to declare variables to be constrained
to be positive so you don't have to do an exp() transform, but then
I see you're creating a log multinormal distribution the theta1IgLogmu, so
that probably won't help. You should see if everything's stable and you're
not getting any rejections during iterations due to arithmetic issues
(shows up in CmdStan as divergences in the print of parameters --- I'm sure
you can fish it out somehow in PyStan or RStan, too).

This:

omegaCorr ~ lkj_corr(1); /////prior for the within-measurement correlation

is implicit because it's uniform on correlation matrices. If you really
want that, you can just remove the sampling statement. All variables are
implicitly uniform on values satisfying their constraints.

This stuff you want to vectorize:

for(i in 1:I){
tau[i] ~ cauchy(0,0.0001); ///prior for the within-measurement scale
igTau[i]~cauchy(0,0.1); ///prior for the within-parameter scale
igCorr[i]~lkj_corr(1.5);

to just

tau ~ cauchy(0, 1e-4);
igTau ~ cauchy(0,1e-1);
for (i in 1:I)
igCorr[i] ~ lkj_corr(1.5);

It's just as efficient, if not more so, to put each variable in its
own loop. It's better for memory locality and loops themselves are
usually pretty much free (that is, it's very unlike R or Python
in terms of what's costly).

That should speed everything up a lot in terms of how long it takes
each iteration. But it won't help convergence (unless there's an issue
with the priors). Tightening priors can help, as can initializing
at a reasonable starting point if convergence is taking a long time.

If you have the WinBUGS code and are worried you've translated it
wrong, we'd be happy to look at pieces.

- Bob
